newsitem.title: FINLAND: ENSKILDA SEES FINLAND, NOT SWEDEN IN EMU.
newsitem.headline: ENSKILDA SEES FINLAND, NOT SWEDEN IN EMU.

text.p: Sweden's Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken predicted on Thursday that Finland, but not Sweden, would be one of eight countries to join Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in the first wave.
"We draw the line right there between Finland and Sweden," Enskilda's Per Jedefors, head of the bank's EMU project, told a seminar on the common European currency here.
Jedefors said the first wave of EMU, due to be launched at the start of 1999, would include eight countries; Germany, France, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, Belgium, Austria, Ireland and Finland.
The forecast was based on the countries' projected fulfilment of the EMU criteria in 1997, and on such factors as public opinion and market sentiment concerning EMU membership.

Though Sweden was on Jedefors's list of "maybes" together with Belgium, Austria, Ireland and Finland, he said he did not expect Sweden to be in EMU right from the start because of broad political opposition in Sweden to EMU.
"We don't think Denmark or the U.K. will join from the beginning, but maybe with some delay," Jedefors added.
"We think this will be a small union -- and a union of countries that can follow the same pace of development," he said.
Enskilda does not expect Portugal, Spain, Italy or Greece to meet the EMU membership criteria, Jedefors said.
Sweden, he said, would not stand to gain any major advantages over Finland by staying outside EMU.

"My view is that the degrees of freedom for economic policy will not be greater outside," he said, adding that Sweden might need to adhere to even more stringent economic policies outside the currency block than it would as member.
"If Sweden doesn't join, the markets will ask why," he said.
Jedefors said Sweden would only stand to benefit from opting out of EMU if the economy were to be hit by an "asymetric shock," and he said that the previous such shock came when Germany was reunited.
